extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the two-part Alice/Mayo §101 analysis for nature-based products and judicial exceptions, including (A) identifying the closest natural counterpart and markedly different characteristics, and (B) determining whether claim elements amount to an inventive concept (significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the closest naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a nature-based product, the examiner must identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart for comparison; do not confuse the counterpart with other material that occurs naturally with or adjacent to the counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For a claimed nucleic acid derived from gene B, the closest counterpart is gene B (not the whole chromosome). For a single-stranded primer derived from a double-stranded nucleic acid, the closest counterpart is the corresponding sense strand. When multiple natural counterparts exist (e.g., cloned animal created from DNA of two breeds), select the counterpart most closely related to the claimed product based on examiner expertise. If the nature-based product is a combination of components with no natural counterpart mixture, compare to the individual naturally occurring components (Funk Bros. example). If claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a best practice for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to assist the applicant and clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics to identify for markedly different analysis must be possessed by the claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics for comparison must be characteristics possessed by the claimed product — the claim defines the invention and thus the characteristics to be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners identify characteristics by reading the claim language and using the broadest reasonable interpretation of the nature-based product. A characteristic may be explicitly recited (e.g., chemical name indicating structural detail) or inferred from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., what nucleotide sequence an 'isolated gene B' encompasses). Unclaimed characteristics cannot be relied upon (Roslin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of appropriate characteristics to consider (structure, function, properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics can be expressed as structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive examples courts consider: biological or pharmacological functions/activities (e.g., protein-encoding information; complementary binding), chemical/physical properties (e.g., alkalinity, ductility), phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), structure and form (physical plasmids, chemical crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype). Specific examples cited: protein encoding (Myriad), binding ability (Ambry), bacterial infection of plants (Funk Bros.), hydrocarbon degradation (Chakrabarty), vitamin C preventing scurvy (King), alkalinity (Parke-Davis), ductility (Marden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claimed product characteristics to counterpart in its natural state
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine if characteristics are 'markedly different,' compare the claimed product’s characteristics to those of the naturally occurring counterpart in the counterpart's natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts emphasize comparison to the natural state; a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be merely inherent or incidental in the counterpart (Myriad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marked difference requires applicant-caused change (not inherent or incidental)
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic is 'markedly different' only if it has been changed relative to the natural counterpart, and that change was caused or produced by the applicant’s efforts or influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is at least one changed characteristic produced by the applicant, that change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic and support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed characteristics and incidental changes do not support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that are incidental to isolation or characteristics that are unclaimed/innate to the natural counterpart cannot be relied upon to show a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Myriad — incidental structural differences from isolation (loss of covalent chromosomal bonds) were not enough where genes were otherwise structurally identical; Ambry — primers' single-stranded creation and their use as starting materials did not create a new function because binding ability was innate; Marden — inherent ductility cannot be treated as a change given by invention; Roslin — phenotypic differences not claimed cannot establish marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language controls what characteristics can be evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: Only characteristics that are recited in the claim or are encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim may be considered in the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected reliance on characteristics not claimed. Examiners should look at explicit claim recitations and at what the claim reasonably encompasses to determine characteristics (e.g., 'deoxyribose' indicates a structural removal of hydroxyl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products found to have markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial examples where claimed nature-based products were found to have markedly different characteristics and thereby eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty bacterium — altered functional capacity (degrades multiple hydrocarbons) and changed structural characteristic (additional plasmids) = eligible. Myriad full-length cDNA — structural change (exons only, introns removed) despite encoding same protein = eligible because cDNA is distinct from genomic DNA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products found to lack markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial examples where claimed products lacked markedly different characteristics and were held to be products of nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad isolated genes — isolation alone did not produce marked differences. Ambry primers — same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function meant no marked difference. Marden ductile vanadium — ductility inherent to vanadium. Roslin animal clones — exact genetic replicas lacked claimed marked differences; phenotypic differences not claimed cannot save eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept: additional elements must supply 'significantly more' than the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), an inventive concept requires elements beyond the exception that, individually or in combination, ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept cannot be the judicial exception itself. It is furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the exception (Alice/Mayo). The search for an inventive concept asks 'what else is there in the claims' beyond the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements both individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether additional elements supply an inventive concept, consider each element alone and the claim elements in combination, because elements that are not sufficient alone may be sufficient in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be considered as a whole (Diamond v. Diehr). Combination of conventional steps arranged non-conventionally may supply an inventive concept (e.g., Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; BASCOM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate inventive concept analysis with novelty or obviousness (35 U.S.C. 102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept (Step 2B) is separate from inquiries of novelty or non-obviousness; novelty/obviousness determinations are distinct and not determinative for §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly warned against substituting §§102/103 inquiries for §101. A new abstract idea is still an abstract idea; lack of novelty under §102 or obviousness under §103 does not automatically indicate the absence of an inventive concept and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations/limitations that have been found to qualify as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations the courts have found to supply significantly more when recited with a judicial exception include improvements to computers or other technologies, use of a particular machine, effecting a transformation, adding specific non-conventional limitations, and other meaningful limitations beyond mere field linkage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative list: (i) improvements to computer functioning (DDR Holdings); (ii) improvements to other technologies/technical fields (Diehr example of thermocouple in rubber molding); (iii) applying the exception with/by use of a particular machine (Fourdrinier arrangement); (iv) effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state (Diehr); (v) adding specific limitations other than well-understood routine conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine to a particular useful application (BASCOM); (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking to a technological environment (Classen immunization step). This list is not exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations/limitations that courts have found insufficient to be 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that do not qualify as significantly more include merely instructing to 'apply it,' generic computer implementation, appending well-understood routine conventional activities at high generality, insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering), and generally linking the exception to a technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) merely adding the words 'apply it' or instructions to implement on a computer (Alice); (ii) appending generic computer functions or well-understood routine conventional activities (Alice); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering (CyberSource); (iv) limiting the abstract idea to a field of use or technological environment without more (Bilski; Parker v. Flook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality or tangibility alone does not establish an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere recitation of a physical or tangible element (e.g., a computer) is not in itself an inventive concept and does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has emphasized that a computer is a tangible machine but mere physical implementation of an exception is not enough; allowing eligibility solely because a computer is recited would make patent eligibility depend on draftsman's art (Alice).
